title: Bank Statement Loans: A Homebuying Path for the Self-Employed
description: If your tax returns don't reflect what your business really earns, a bank statement loan may help. Here's how these non-QM loans work and who they fit best.
image_alt: A woman working at a table covered in papers and documents

faq.q: What is a bank statement loan?
faq.a: It's a non-QM mortgage that uses your business or personal bank deposits, typically over 12 or 24 months, to estimate income instead of relying on tax returns.

faq.q: Are bank statement loans more expensive?
faq.a: They usually carry higher pricing than conventional loans because they fall outside agency guidelines. Many borrowers use them as a bridge and refinance later if their tax returns support it.

faq.q: Who qualifies for a bank statement loan?
faq.a: Typically self-employed borrowers with a business history of around two years, solid credit, and enough down payment and reserves. Requirements vary by lender.

body_html:
Business owners are often great at one thing that hurts them on a mortgage application: lowering their taxable income. Every legitimate deduction that saves money on taxes also shrinks the income a traditional lender can use. That's how successful people end up being told they qualify for far less house than they can comfortably afford.

Bank statement loans were built for exactly this situation.

How a bank statement loan works

Instead of using tax returns, the lender reviews 12 or 24 months of bank statements and calculates income from your deposits. For business accounts, an expense factor is applied to account for costs of doing business, or the lender may use a profit and loss statement prepared by a CPA or tax preparer. Personal account statements can sometimes be used at full deposit value if business income flows there.

Because these loans fall outside Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac guidelines, they're considered non-QM, or non-qualified mortgages. That doesn't mean risky or unregulated. Lenders still must verify your ability to repay; they just use different evidence to do it.

Who they fit best

  • Self-employed borrowers with significant write-offs
  • Small business owners whose income has grown recently
  • 1099 contractors and gig workers with consistent deposits
  • Real estate agents, consultants, and other commission-heavy professionals

What lenders typically look for

AreaWhat to expect
Business historyOften around two years of self-employment, verified by a license, CPA letter, or filings
Statements12 or 24 consecutive months, all pages
DepositsLarge or unusual deposits may need explanation
CreditPricing improves with stronger credit
Down payment and reservesUsually more than agency loans require

The trade-offs to understand

Bank statement loans generally cost more than conventional financing, and down payment expectations are higher. Many of my clients treat them as a bridge: buy the home now, then refinance into a conventional loan in a couple of years once tax returns reflect stronger income. Ask about any prepayment penalty before you commit, especially if refinancing later is part of the plan.

How to prepare

  1. Separate business and personal accounts. Clean statements make income calculation easier and faster.
  2. Keep deposits explainable. Transfers between your own accounts, loans, and one-time windfalls can complicate the math.
  3. Talk to your CPA early. Some programs use a CPA-prepared P&L, and timing your tax filings can matter.
  4. Compare against traditional options first. Sometimes a conventional loan still works using two years of returns. Check before assuming you need non-QM.

A sample walk-through of the process

Here's how a typical bank statement purchase moves from first call to closing, so you know what to expect.

  1. Scenario review. We talk about your business, how long you've owned it, how income flows into your accounts, and the price range you're considering. This is where we decide between business and personal statements, and between 12 and 24 months.
  2. Statement analysis. You send complete statements, every page, for the chosen period. We calculate qualifying income using the lender's method, and flag any deposits that will need an explanation.
  3. Lender comparison. Because non-QM guidelines differ so much, we compare several lenders on income calculation, down payment, reserves, and prepayment terms. The same file can produce noticeably different results from one lender to the next.
  4. Pre-approval. Once the numbers are solid, you get a pre-approval letter that reflects the actual program. That letter carries the same weight in an offer as any other.
  5. Escrow. Underwriting verifies the business, reviews the statements again, and orders the appraisal. Expect a few follow-up questions about deposits; quick answers keep things moving.

Questions to ask any lender

  • How is the expense factor determined for my type of business?
  • Can personal and business statements be combined?
  • Is there a prepayment penalty, and how long does it last?
  • What reserves are required after closing?
  • If my tax returns improve, what would a future refinance look like?

Good answers to these questions tell you a lot about whether a program fits your plans, not just whether you qualify today.

The takeaway

If you've been told "your tax returns don't support it," that's not the end of the conversation. A bank statement loan may let your real cash flow tell the story. As a broker, I can compare several non-QM lenders at once, which matters because their guidelines vary more than most. If your debt-to-income ratio looks tight on paper, this is worth a closer look.
